routes.description: Establish that universally binding moral truths require a nonhuman objective standard, identify that standard with God's immutable and revealed character, and show that secular welfare, preference, convention, and contract accounts cannot supply equivalent moral objectivity or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective moral absolutes are established, God's necessary character is shown to ground both their truth and authority, and the proposed secular standards are shown unable to explain their universality, nonarbitrariness, or prescriptive force.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral truth and obligation require God's character as their necessary, nonhuman foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that at least some actions possess universally true moral status independent of individual or collective preference.
Explain how God's immutable character, rather than an arbitrary divine choice, constitutes the objective moral standard.
Show why consequence, preference, convention, and contractual agreement cannot generate universally binding moral duties.
Connect God's nature, creative authority, and purposes to prescriptions that bind human agents.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how revelation and divine omniscience provide access to moral requirements and informed guidance about their application.
Use difficult cases to test whether harm-oriented secular standards preserve the moral judgments they purport to explain.

routes.description: Reject the claimed necessity of a divine foundation by distinguishing definitions from objectively assessable judgments, grounding moral inquiry in real consequences, intentions, and impartial rule construction, and showing that divine-nature claims do not independently explain goodness or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a coherent secular method can yield objective assessments or justified rules without God, or if the divine account fails to establish moral absolutes, nonarbitrary goodness, or a valid transition from facts about God to binding duties.

motionBridge.description: Show that God is not required for defensible moral truth or obligation because secular inquiry is viable or divine grounding is explanatorily incomplete.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish the selection of a moral standard from the objective truth of judgments concerning suffering, consequences, intentions, and circumstances.
Explain how welfare-sensitive reasoning and impartial contractual construction can justify rules without presupposing divine existence.
Test whether identifying goodness with God's nature makes the divine standard circular, arbitrary, or modally unexplained.
Require an account of how descriptions of God's nature, power, creation, or judgment entail reasons or duties to obey.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish God's possible role as an omniscient source of information from the facts that make conduct morally right or wrong.
Separate the existence or justification of moral requirements from motivation, compliance, punishment, and practical deterrence.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and the Existence of Absolutes
sections.rationale: Defines the phenomenon requiring explanation and tests whether morality involves intrinsic universal truths, objectively assessable claims under a chosen standard, or context-sensitive judgments about consequences and intentions.

sections.title: Divine Nature, Necessity, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: Addresses whether God's immutable character supplies a necessary moral standard or leaves unresolved circularity, contrary-nature possibilities, and the basis for calling the divine character good.

sections.title: Secular Welfare and Impartial Rule Construction
sections.rationale: Examines whether facts about suffering, potential conscious states, social consequences, and veil-of-ignorance reasoning can support objective assessments or justified rules without God.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and the Is-Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: Tests how either foundation produces binding prescriptions, with particular attention to whether creation, ownership, divine purposes, definitions, or secular commitments provide reasons agents ought to act.

sections.title: Omniscience, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Distinguishes the metaphysical ground of morality from access to relevant facts and evaluates whether omniscience and revelation establish foundation, reliable guidance, or only informational authority.

sections.title: Counterexamples, Motivation, and Practical Force
sections.rationale: Organizes the disputed cases involving hidden harm, rule consequences, disobedience, punishment, and deterrence to test each account without conflating moral truth with motivation or compliance.

routes.description: Establish that spacetime and material appearances emerge from a more fundamental informational or relational reality, that this foundation is better understood as mental than material, and that a necessary perfect mind provides the most economical ultimate ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if emergent-spacetime and structural considerations support an information-first ontology, the transition from information to mentality is warranted, and a necessary divine mind explains consciousness, regularity, and contingency more economically than materialist alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that theistic idealism provides a simpler and more adequate ultimate explanation of emergent physical reality than materialist realism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that experienced spacetime and material structure are nonfundamental and emerge from deeper informational, mathematical, or relational structure.
Explain why an informational or structural foundation is more plausibly mental than a mind-independent physical substrate.
Show why the foundational mind should be understood as necessary and perfect rather than finite, contingent, or merely simulator-like.
Demonstrate that one foundational mind introduces fewer unexplained entities and brute facts than a material foundation plus emergent consciousness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use quantum-gravity, holographic, quantum-cognition, and structural-realist considerations to support the proposed emergence and mentality premises.
Specify how scientific findings can alter the comparative probability of the metaphysical account even without strictly entailing or falsifying it.

routes.description: Maintain that frontier physics neither establishes emergent spacetime nor connects any such emergence to mentality, while materialist realism supplies concrete relata and causal constraints without adding a divine mind whose choices leave the world underdetermined.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the scientific evidence remains compatible with nonmental foundations, the inference from mathematical structure to idealism is blocked, and materialist realism proves comparatively simpler or more discriminating than theistic idealism.

motionBridge.description: Show that materialist realism is the simpler and better-disciplined explanation because the available physics does not preferentially support a divine mental foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that emergent-spacetime and holographic research remains unsettled or compatible with multiple nonidealist interpretations.
Show that mathematical, informational, or relational descriptions do not eliminate concrete physical relata or entail a mental ontology.
Provide a coherent impersonal physical or quantum foundation capable of generating spacetime and consciousness without divine agency.
Demonstrate that stable material properties constrain possible outcomes more effectively than unrestricted libertarian divine choices.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use the success of physical theories to justify realist commitment to an underlying physical structure or substrate.
Distinguish a first cause or productive timeless foundation from a being possessing mentality and perfect-being attributes.

sections.title: Evidence for Emergent Spacetime
sections.rationale: The scientific status and scope of spacetime emergence determine whether the pro route has its initial premise and whether the con route can retain a fundamental or deeper physical basis.

sections.title: From Structure and Information to Ontology
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether structural realism, mathematical description, and information-first physics favor idealism or instead presuppose concrete physical relata described by successful theories.

sections.title: From Emergence to Mind and God
sections.rationale: The motion requires more than nonfundamental spacetime; it requires a warranted transition to mentality, agency, necessity, and the attributes distinguishing God from an impersonal first cause.

sections.title: Parsimony, Contingency, and Brute Facts
sections.rationale: The competing routes centrally dispute whether a necessary perfect mind reduces unexplained foundations or whether divine freedom adds unconstrained choices while retaining all physical regularities.

sections.title: Explanatory Constraint and Empirical Discrimination
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether either worldview favors some observations over others, identifies meaningful defeaters, and explains actual regularity rather than merely accommodating every possibility.

routes.description: Show that publicly testable scientific explanation can account for cosmic and biological development, consciousness, morality, and future intelligence without divine agency, while evidence for supernatural claims, cosmic purpose, and an afterlife remains insufficient.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if scientific materialism offers adequate natural explanations or disciplined research programs for the debate's central phenomena, answers claims that value and personhood require transcendence, and supports a credible account of meaning and responsible technological development without God.

motionBridge.description: Establish that science and naturalistic explanation make divine agency unnecessary while providing sufficient resources for humanity's future.

centralBridges.description: Defend public evidence and corrigible inquiry as the appropriate standards, then show how cosmology and evolution progressively replace supernatural explanations of origins and complexity.
Account for consciousness, moral behavior, personhood, and finite human purposes within material nature and evolutionary history without requiring transcendent grounding.
Explain how materialism can recognize advanced artificial intelligence and guide genetic or other technological development through concern for present flourishing and avoidance of harm.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test resurrection, miracle, afterlife, and revelation claims against evidential standards and distinguish symbolic usefulness from historical truth.
Show why unsupported religious promises or cosmic-purpose claims may impede inquiry or depreciate present human aspirations.

routes.description: Show that science powerfully explains material mechanisms but does not exhaust questions of existence, moral obligation, meaning, relational personhood, or hope, and that Christian theism can integrate established science with a creator, historical claims, and an ethics of human dignity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the limits of scientific materialism are established without rejecting evolutionary science, Christian knowledge claims receive a coherent evidential basis, and the resulting account of value, personhood, hope, and technological responsibility addresses humanity's future.

motionBridge.description: Establish that scientific explanation remains compatible with and incomplete without the Christian account of origins, value, personhood, and hope.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish explanations of material operation from questions of why anything exists and why moral obligations, meaning, and value have authority.
Integrate evolution and revisable interpretations of scripture with an originating and sustaining creator without treating unresolved science as direct proof of God.
Ground relational human dignity and apply it to artificial intelligence, genetic intervention, unequal access, disability, and the protection of vulnerable people.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how a transcendent God could be known through self-revelation and defend the resurrection as a historically serious central Christian claim.
Show how Christian affirmation of the physical world and future hope can motivate scientific investigation and responsible action in the present.

sections.title: Epistemic Scope and Supernatural Evidence
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether scientific inquiry answers every real question or only material mechanisms, and whether revelation, resurrection, and miracle claims meet defensible standards of knowledge.

sections.title: Cosmic and Biological Origins
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether cosmology and evolution remove explanatory need for God or remain compatible with a creator and leave ultimate existence unresolved.

sections.title: Morality, Meaning, and Hope
sections.rationale: This issue compares evolutionary and chosen accounts of ethics and purpose with claims that obligation, value, afterlife, and future hope require or gain coherence from transcendence.

sections.title: Personhood, Artificial Intelligence, and Genetic Technology
sections.rationale: This issue applies the rival accounts of human nature and dignity to artificial intelligence, enhancement, healing, unequal access, disability, and humanity's technological future.

sections.title: Science, Faith, and Human Flourishing
sections.rationale: This issue assesses whether religion obstructs evidence-based progress or can coexist with scientific practice and motivate investigation, ethical restraint, and responsible present action.

routes.description: Establish that logic, truth, induction, ethics, and knowledge are mutually dependent transcendental preconditions whose intelligibility requires a unified metaphysical ground, and identify the Orthodox Christian God as that necessary ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it establishes both that non-theistic accounts cannot coherently justify the named transcendental preconditions and that the Orthodox account positively and necessarily explains their reality, normativity, stability, and interrelation.

motionBridge.description: Show that Orthodox Christian theism is necessary, rather than merely compatible with or explanatorily attractive for, grounding logic, truth, induction, ethics, and knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Establish that rational thought, predication, inquiry, communication, and action unavoidably presuppose the named transcendental categories.
Show that skeptical, empiricist, pragmatic, materialist, and secular stopping points cannot justify the categories they employ without circularity, arbitrariness, or self-defeat.
Explain how the personal divine mind, Logos, and providence jointly ground universals, truth, logical invariance, natural regularity, moral norms, and knowability.
Establish why the required ground is specifically the Orthodox Christian God and not an unspecified deity, primitive necessity, or another metaphysical system.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend transcendental proof through the claim that denying necessary preconditions already relies upon them, and explain its relation to coherentist rather than classical foundationalist justification.
Resolve objections concerning induction's circularity and whether logical laws are independent of God, arbitrarily created, or reflections of divine action.

routes.description: Deny that the transcendental argument establishes the necessity of Orthodox Christian theism by separating justified use of logic, truth, induction, ethics, and knowledge from possession of an ultimate divine explanation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the demand for a further ground, the inference to any deity, or the inference to Orthodox Christianity remains unestablished, while a fallible non-theistic account permits rational reliance on the disputed categories.

motionBridge.description: Show that the transcendental argument does not establish Orthodox Christian theism as a necessary ground for logic, truth, induction, ethics, or knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Require a clear argument establishing that the categories need an external ground, that a divine ground follows, and that all relevant non-theistic alternatives are excluded.
Provide a fallibilist account on which persistent reliability, shared reality, parsimony, and proportioned confidence justify rational inquiry without absolute certainty.
Maintain that logical relations may be necessary, primitive, or descriptive of reality, so their indispensability does not entail a separate divine guarantor.
Show that positing God may relocate the presupposition and does not by itself explain logical necessity, secure fallible human access, or identify Orthodox Christianity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish uncertainty and nonbelief from assertions that no foundation or deity exists, preserving the affirmative side's burden to demonstrate necessity.
Account for practical logical norms, evidential judgment, and moral conclusions through secular reasons and methods without presupposing a theistic foundation.

sections.title: Necessity of an Orthodox theistic ground
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on the motion-level inference from the existence or indispensability of transcendental categories to the necessity of God, including whether Orthodox theism is uniquely required rather than merely one possible explanation.

sections.title: Logic, necessity, and the divine mind
sections.rationale: The relation between logical laws and God is a central test of the proposed ground: the issue includes whether logic reflects the divine mind or divine energies, is independent of God, or may be treated as necessarily invariant without an additional guarantor.

sections.title: Knowledge, certainty, and fallible access
sections.rationale: The motion concerns knowledge and truth, making it necessary to address whether ultimate metaphysical grounding is required for warranted belief, whether fallible confidence is sufficient, and whether a perfect ground would resolve human cognitive limitations.

sections.title: Induction, natural regularity, and science
sections.rationale: Induction is expressly within the motion and supplies a concrete clash over whether observed reliability can justify continued inference or whether the regularity presupposed by science requires divine providence and transcendental explanation.

sections.title: Transcendental proof, coherentism, and argument form
sections.rationale: This issue concerns how the proposed argument is meant to establish its conclusion: through denial-dependent proof, holistic worldview comparison, and coherentism, or through explicit premises that demonstrate necessity and exclude relevant alternatives.

sections.title: Worldview commitments, ethics, and skeptical neutrality
sections.rationale: The remaining burden-relevant dispute concerns whether nonbelief or suspended judgment still carries metaphysical, logical, and ethical commitments, and whether practical or secular reasons can account for rational and moral norms without the proposed theistic foundation.

routes.description: Establish that people sometimes face genuinely available alternatives, exercise control over which alternative occurs, and thereby possess the kind of freedom capable of grounding responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by supporting alternatives and agent control, answering the inference from pervasive causal influence to exhaustive determination, and connecting that freedom to deliberation, normative requirements, and desert-sensitive responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that genuine alternatives and control sometimes exist and can justify responsibility for the action selected.

centralBridges.description: Explain why causal influence, probabilistic pressure, and reason-giving explanation need not eliminate every genuinely available alternative.
Supply a defensible basis for believing in freedom while addressing challenges to intuition, appearances, deliberation, and reason-responsive belief.
Show why responsibility and normative practices require feasible alternatives or desert beyond purely forward-looking behavioral management.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the incompatibilist and possible compatibilist concepts at stake when control, fixed history, and the ability to do otherwise are compared.
Explain how reasons can make free action intelligible even if the final selection is not determined by a further cause.

routes.description: Establish that behavior remains within an integrated chain of biological and environmental causes, leaving no agent-controlled selection among genuinely available alternatives and no desert-based responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting multi-timescale causal explanation to the exclusion of libertarian control, rebutting intuition-based and practical objections, and deriving responsibility practices that do not depend on retribution or earned moral entitlement.

motionBridge.description: Show that antecedent causation excludes genuine alternative control and therefore cannot justify desert-based responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Integrate immediate, neural, physiological, developmental, genetic, cultural, and historical causes into a continuous account of behavior.
Explain why expanding mechanistic evidence and the absence of causally independent action undermine reliance on experienced freedom.
Show how learning, intervention, deliberative inputs, and behavioral change can operate causally without agent-originating freedom.
Connect causal explanation to rejection of retribution and differential desert while preserving forward-looking social responses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish agent control from randomness so that indeterminacy does not itself establish freely authored choice.
Account for gratitude and other responsibility-adjacent practices through evolutionary and mechanistic functions without presupposing free choice.

sections.title: Causal explanation, influence, and genuinely available alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the integrated biological and environmental causal account exhausts the explanation of conduct or merely influences choices while leaving some alternatives available.

sections.title: Intuition, scientific evidence, and the burden of proof
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether experienced freedom and intellectual appearances supply a rational default, or whether mechanistic discoveries and historical error require withholding or revising that belief.

sections.title: Control, deliberation, change, and reason-responsive agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deliberation, advice, belief formation, learning, and reasons can constitute meaningful control or remain fully intelligible as determined causal processes.

sections.title: Responsibility, moral desert, punishment, and humane practice
sections.rationale: This issue connects the metaphysical dispute to the motion's responsibility clause by testing retribution, innocence, entitlement, blame, and forward-looking approaches to harmful behavior.

sections.title: Concepts of freedom, explanatory stopping points, and indeterminacy
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies incompatibilist and compatibilist definitions, whether choice can terminate explanation at an agent's reasons, and why randomness alone may fail to provide agency.

routes.description: Establish that a necessary supreme mental foundation gives a more unified and no more complex account of ultimate reality, necessary domains, consciousness, and relevant worldview consequences than a limited naturalistic initial reality.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the supreme-foundation account avoids unexplained arbitrary limitations, derives burden-relevant attributes and consequences from a unified basis, and explains mind without incurring greater whole-worldview complexity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the supreme mental foundation provides the better comparative account of ultimate reality, mind, and worldview simplicity.

centralBridges.description: Show that unexplained limitations on necessary initial reality add primitives or information that an unlimited supreme foundation can avoid.
Establish that supreme value supports the substantive attributes and consequences required for a recognizably theistic explanatory foundation.
Show that deriving necessary logical, moral, mental, and causal domains from one basis has explanatory value over independent foundations.
Show that conscious properties resist strict physical identity and fit an ultimate mental foundation better than a wholly nonmental origin.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify that a theistic foundation can share a broad concrete category with created reality without depending on a supernatural label.
Justify focused property-level comparisons as informative components of an eventual comparison between complete worldviews.

routes.description: Establish that a necessary naturalistic initial reality, assessed within the complete worldview, avoids unwarranted additions of mentality and divine structure while remaining compatible with physical continuity, independent necessary domains, and a neural account of consciousness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the theistic derivation from unlimitedness to supreme personhood remains unsupported, naturalism supplies an adequate account of initial reality and mind, and whole-worldview comparison gives no simplicity-based reason to prefer the theistic foundation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the naturalistic initial-reality account provides the better comparative account once total commitments and relevant data are considered.

centralBridges.description: Show that consciousness, supremacy, and personhood are positive additions rather than consequences of merely removing arbitrary limitations.
Defend necessary initial reality as an explanatory stopping point whose further properties should remain open to warranted scientific inquiry.
Show that causal initiality need not furnish a single common ground for logic, value, consciousness, and every other necessary domain.
Provide a physical identity account of consciousness that accommodates introspective knowledge and the broader behavioral and neurological evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish broad causal continuity between the necessary initial physical reality and the later temporal manifold.
Require local simplicity and explanatory claims to survive comparison of the rival worldviews' complete commitments and consequences.

sections.title: Initial Reality, Naturalness, and Categorical Continuity
sections.rationale: The competing definitions of natural reality and the claimed continuity between an ultimate foundation and later concrete reality determine what the motion's alternatives include and whether either incurs a categorical cost.

sections.title: Arbitrary Limits, Supreme Value, and Personhood
sections.rationale: The central inference from an unrestricted necessary foundation to supreme value, mentality, and personhood bears directly on whether the theistic proposal is simpler or instead adds unsupported structure.

sections.title: Necessity, Unification, and Explanatory Stopping Points
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether necessity ends explanation, whether necessary features remain theoretical primitives, and whether one unified foundation is preferable to several independent necessary domains.

sections.title: Consciousness, Introspection, and Physical Identity
sections.rationale: The dispute over introspection, phenomenal properties, and neural identity is essential to whether mind requires a mental ultimate foundation or can be accommodated within naturalistic reality.

sections.title: Local Analysis and Whole-Worldview Comparison
sections.rationale: The governing comparative method determines how foundational simplicity, explanatory reach, predictions, and focused examples contribute to the motion without substituting isolated considerations for complete-worldview assessment.

routes.description: Present objective moral facts and duties, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and moral rationality as a connected body of evidence, then compare classical theism with secular ethical accounts under abductive explanatory criteria.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the four moral phenomena warrant explanation, classical theism is a legitimate explanatory candidate, and its account of their authority, accessibility, transformative horizon, and relation to fulfillment provides qualified comparative support for theism.

motionBridge.description: Comparative explanation of the four moral phenomena must provide at least a qualified increase in the plausibility of classical theism within a cumulative case.

centralBridges.description: Objective value and categorical obligation, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and morality’s rational relation to fulfillment must be established as genuine explananda.
A morally perfect, omniscient, and omnipotent creator must qualify as a coherent candidate capable of explaining the identified moral phenomena.
The theistic account must explain the authority and breadth of moral experience better than naturalistic, cultural, instrumental, or axiomatic alternatives.
The comparative advantage must remain evidentially relevant after accounting for prior plausibility, an incomplete candidate pool, combined alternatives, and the argument’s cumulative role.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Moral phenomenology and properly basic moral apprehension must support irreducible categorical authority rather than merely chosen goals or social conditioning.
Theism must offer resources for complete moral transformation and for harmony between moral life and ultimate human fulfillment.

routes.description: Challenge both the proposed moral explananda and the admission of God into the explanatory comparison while showing how well-being, empathy, culture, natural processes, and disciplined inquiry can account for moral judgment and change.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism lacks demonstrated candidacy or comparative explanatory advantage, or if secular accounts adequately accommodate the four moral phenomena while theistic grounding leaves additional epistemic, methodological, or hiddenness problems.

motionBridge.description: The four moral phenomena must fail to provide a warranted comparative inference from moral experience to classical theism.

centralBridges.description: God’s eligibility and the adequacy of the explanatory candidate pool must be justified before comparative abduction can support a theistic conclusion.
Well-being, empathy, shared physical needs, learning, culture, and natural processes must adequately explain moral evaluation, conscience, knowledge, and ordinary transformation.
Objective means-end assessment after adopting foundational values must remain viable without an additional divine source of categorical obligation.
Problems of divine identification, access to divine requirements, unconstrained supernatural hypotheses, and hiddenness must defeat the claimed theistic advantage.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Variation in guilt and moral intuition must support cultural and psychological explanations rather than an inference to universally apprehended divine authority.
Any comparative conclusion must be constrained by priors, bad-lot concerns, combined secular alternatives, and the limited reach of moral intuition.

sections.title: Abductive Method, Candidate Pool, and Conclusion
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether classical theism may enter the explanatory comparison, how candidate-pool and prior-plausibility constraints apply, and what qualified conclusion comparative success could support.

sections.title: Objective Moral Facts and Categorical Authority
sections.rationale: The principal ontological clash concerns whether binding moral obligations are irreducibly categorical and call for a personal moral ground, or can be understood through foundational values and objective relations to well-being.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Guilt, and Conscience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether moral axioms, guilt, and apparent authority disclose genuine moral truths requiring theistic explanation or arise adequately through empathy, culture, learning, and shared human conditions.

sections.title: Moral Transformation and Its Horizon
sections.rationale: Transformation is an express part of the motion, requiring comparison between theistic hope for complete moral formation and secular mechanisms that produce behavioral and character change.

sections.title: Moral Rationality, Flourishing, and Scope
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether morality is rationally congruent with ultimate fulfillment and whether flourishing-based accounts can cover categorical duties, animal suffering, character, and apparent conflicts between morality and self-interest.

sections.title: Comparative Worldview Fit and Theistic Liabilities
sections.rationale: The final comparison integrates explanatory breadth with challenges involving divine identification, access, methodological restraint, hiddenness, naturalistic reduction, and the cumulative evidential role claimed for morality.

routes.description: Establish that a broadly Christian society provides more durable foundations and stronger practical support for beneficial institutions, social conduct, human welfare, liberty, and intergenerational continuity than secular ethics.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian commitments are connected to socially important institutions and outcomes, those benefits are shown to remain distinctively dependent on Christianity, and secular ethics is shown unable to equal or sustain them over time.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity yields a more beneficial and sustainable social order than secular ethics across the debate's principal institutional, moral, and human-welfare criteria.

centralBridges.description: Establish a credible comparative connection between Christian practice and prosocial behavior, charitable institutions, mental health, liberty, and resistance to authoritarian politics.
Show that Christianity materially generated or preserved the legal, educational, medical, scientific, and human-rights institutions central to modern social flourishing.
Explain why Christian anthropology and moral commitments provide a durable basis for equal worth, fallibility, responsibility, and humane social norms.
Demonstrate that demographic and cultural continuity is a necessary condition for preserving beneficial institutions and that Christian society better satisfies it.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the methodological relevance of sociological findings by connecting measured religiosity and study populations specifically to practiced Christianity.
Identify Christian ideas about fallibility, lawful creation, and common human ancestry that could explain the claimed institutional and ethical effects.

routes.description: Establish that secular ethics offers an adequate moral foundation and a more reliable method for building a free, humane, knowledgeable, and revisable society than dependence on Christian doctrine or Christian-majority identity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if secular ethics can ground dignity and cooperation, empirical inquiry and fallibilism are connected to modern social gains, and Christianity's alleged unique benefits are shown to be unnecessary, overstated, or offset by doctrinal and historical costs.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular ethics better supports humane social outcomes through equal standing, open inquiry, empirical correction, and revisable moral deliberation without requiring Christian authority.

centralBridges.description: Provide a sufficient secular basis for equal human worth, reciprocity, empathy, cooperation, responsibility, and rational consideration of consequences.
Connect secular Enlightenment norms and empirical inquiry to modern freedom, science, reduced violence, expanded equality, and correction of harmful supernatural explanations.
Establish that Christian doctrines or institutions can impose coercion, inherited guilt, exclusion, dogmatism, or historically harmful practices relevant to social comparison.

Show that beneficial institutions and conduct attributed to Christianity can arise from secular methods, while Christian identity and religiosity are too heterogeneous to establish general superiority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how open criticism and willingness to revise beliefs constrain both religious dogma and dogmatic secular political movements.
Distinguish the historical Christian setting of modern institutions from the present justification and operation of their secular empirical methods.

sections.title: Comparative Social and Psychological Outcomes
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparison of lived social effects, making charity, volunteering, health, interpersonal conduct, and the reliability and Christian specificity of the supporting research a major burden-bearing clash.

sections.title: Origins and Operation of Modern Institutions
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of science, education, medicine, rights, democracy, and Enlightenment reform determine whether modern social gains depend on Christianity or are better explained and maintained by secular inquiry.

sections.title: Foundations of Morality, Dignity, and Cooperation
sections.rationale: Each side must explain how its framework supports equal worth, moral obligation, empathy, responsibility, and cooperative life, including whether those goods require divine authority or can rest on shared humanity and deliberation.

sections.title: Doctrine, Dogma, and Corrective Fallibilism
sections.rationale: The social implications of original sin, punishment, scriptural authority, naturalism, open questioning, and belief revision bear on which framework better prevents coercion and corrects moral or factual error.

sections.title: Political Liberty and Social Continuity
sections.rationale: Claims about authoritarianism, Christian nationalism, demographic sustainability, cultural persistence, and the relevance of fertility test whether either framework can preserve free and beneficial institutions across generations.

routes.description: Establish that religious explanations and institutions replace warranted uncertainty with unsupported supernatural certainty, distort accounts of nature and morality, and generate avoidable harms that secular inquiry and responsibility can address.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if religion is shown to be epistemically unnecessary and materially harmful across the debate's principal explanatory, moral, existential, and political domains, while secular alternatives preserve inquiry, responsibility, solidarity, and meaning.

motionBridge.description: Connect religious claims of revelation, providence, and authority to avoidable intellectual, moral, or political harms while showing that abandoning them does not sacrifice necessary explanation or value.

centralBridges.description: Show that doubt, falsifiability, and open inquiry provide a sounder method than revelation, unfalsifiable explanation, or claims of settled divine purpose.
Show that cosmology, biology, and human origins can be addressed without purposeful design and that generic causal inference does not establish an interventionist religious deity.
Account for morality, purpose, solidarity, transcendence, and acceptance of mortality without supernatural command, judgment, or promised immortality.
Explain how divine warrants, providential interpretation, and absolutist authority can intensify conflict, repression, fear, or moral distortion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use religious diversity, geographic inheritance, and human psychological projection as supporting reasons to treat religions as human constructions rather than unified revelation.
Illustrate how evidence-based causal accounts displace supernatural interpretations of disease, catastrophe, cosmic history, and biological development.

routes.description: Establish the God hypothesis as a rational explanatory framework for cosmic and biological order, moral and religious experience, purpose, and causal origins, while separating religion from harms attributed to human agency or secular ideology.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism supplies a coherent and comparatively economical account of the debate's major explanatory and existential facts, can answer methodological objections, and need not bear primary responsibility for the cited violence and suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that a divine source makes life, order, morality, purpose, and experience more intelligible than secular doubt and that the alleged harms do not establish religion itself as the governing problem.

centralBridges.description: Infer intelligence or supernatural causation from the origin of life, life-permitting physical conditions, nature's intelligibility, and patterned biological outcomes.
Explain altruism, moral obligation, and persistent religious experience in ways that require more than evolutionary advantage, social inheritance, or mass error.
Preserve a distinct explanatory role for religion concerning purpose, destiny, death, and practical commitment beyond scientific descriptions of physical mechanism.
Distinguish religious belief from conquest, voluntary human evil, and secular utopian violence so that historical harm is assigned to the relevant human or ideological causes.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Answer unfalsifiability and parsimony objections by identifying assessable religious claims and comparing the commitments of divine and naturalistic alternatives.
Maintain that a belief's psychological, social, or geographic origin does not determine its truth and that competing claims require substantive comparison.

sections.title: Inquiry, Revelation, and the Testability of Religious Claims
sections.rationale: This issue determines the governing method for comparing the God hypothesis with secular doubt, including whether revelation and religious explanation expose themselves to meaningful evidential tests or improperly convert uncertainty into certainty.

sections.title: Cosmic Origins, Life, and the Inference to Design
sections.rationale: The explanatory comparison over causation, fine-tuning, abiogenesis, evolutionary contingency, convergence, and planetary habitability is a principal route for deciding whether God adds necessary explanatory value to accounts of life and the universe.

sections.title: Morality, Altruism, and Human Responsibility
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing religious and secular accounts of moral obligation, aid to strangers, ethical responsibility, and the extent to which moral conduct depends on divine command or supernatural accountability.

sections.title: Purpose, Mortality, Faith, and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether religion uniquely explains meaning, destiny, transcendence, practical commitment, and widespread religious experience, or whether finite secular life can sustain those experiences and purposes without supernatural judgment.

sections.title: Religious Authority, Providence, and Political Violence
sections.rationale: The direct claim that religion is the problem turns substantially on whether divine warrants, prophecy, and absolutist authority cause or intensify violence and repression, or whether the relevant harms arise from human agency, conquest, and secular ideologies.

moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the pro side's governing contrast between revisable inquiry and revelation's asserted settlement of disputed questions.

charity.alternative: Revelation may initiate rather than dissolve continuing moral and historical reasoning.

moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens

precisionFindings.rationale: The contemporary examples and claimed divine warrants are clear, with only an implicit limitation to the identified actors and conflicts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support the bounded claim that divine warrants can legitimize violence, without requiring that religion be its sole cause.

routes.description: Establish that naturally developed, reasons-responsive self-control constitutes the freedom relevant to moral agency and can support ordinary desert, responsibility, sanctions, and reactive practices without requiring ultimate self-creation or indeterminism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects practical control and moral competence to meaningful alternatives, distinguishes ordinary causation from responsibility-undermining interference, and explains why stable responsibility practices and proportionate consequences remain justified under determinism.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control is sufficient to justify compatibilist freedom, ordinary desert, and responsibility practices.

centralBridges.description: Define the relevant freedom through informed, unimpaired, reasons-responsive self-control rather than randomness or ultimate metaphysical authorship.
Explain how learning, reflection, practice, and moral education make agents sufficiently autonomous and accountable despite deterministic causal histories.
Justify proportionate, public, rule-governed sanctions and blame as components of a secure cooperative social order.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish deliberate interpersonal control from impersonal causal determination in assessing whether an agent's control has been displaced.
Account for morally condemnatory reactions as fitting and behavior-guiding responses to serious wrongdoing by competent adults.

routes.description: Establish that reasons-responsive agency does not supply the ultimate control required for basic desert, while showing that protection, deterrence, rehabilitation, moral engagement, and rule enforcement remain available on forward-looking grounds.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it separates practical agency from basic-desert responsibility, shows why neither determinism nor indeterminism supplies ultimate control, and provides non-desert foundations for justified social responses without retaining retribution or desert-dependent anger.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control does not justify basic desert and that defensible responsibility practices need not presuppose it.

centralBridges.description: Argue that agents are not ultimate sources of their characters and actions under either deterministic or indeterministic causal conditions.
Show that reasons-responsiveness and compatibilist agent control can matter practically without establishing desert-based blame or punishment.
Ground coercion, deterrence, rehabilitation, and rule enforcement in public safety, future risk, proportionality, and least-restrictive means.
Require an independent role for backward-looking desert beyond what consequentialist institutions and causal responsibility already provide.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use manipulation and malfunction cases to test whether internal psychological responsiveness is sufficient for responsibility.
Explain how evolved reactive attitudes and responsibility practices can be revised without surrendering their protective or communicative functions.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Control and the Ability to Do Otherwise
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether informed, unimpaired responsiveness to reasons constitutes the relevant practical control and meaningful alternative possibilities, or whether those capacities fall short of the freedom needed for desert.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Determinism, and Manipulation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deterministic histories undermine accountable agency, whether developed self-control supplies adequate sourcehood, and whether manipulation cases reveal a relevant gap between causation and control.

sections.title: Basic Desert and Ordinary Compatibilist Desert
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the central conceptual dispute over whether basic desert is required, whether ordinary conduct-sensitive desert is independently defensible, and whether reasons-responsive agency can bridge the two notions.

sections.title: Punishment, Public Safety, and Institutional Justification
sections.rationale: This issue compares rule-governed punishment and proportional sanctions with quarantine, deterrence, rehabilitation, and least-restrictive protection as foundations for legitimate coercive practices.

sections.title: Reactive Attitudes and Reform of Responsibility Practices
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether moral anger and condemnation are justified or indispensable, and whether evolved practices can instead be revised toward non-desert attitudes while retaining social regulation and moral communication.
